name: Sega Dreamcast
tierWhy: Sega decided on January 31, 2001 to stop making the Dreamcast and left the console hardware business; Sega itself survives as a software publisher inside Sega Sammy Holdings, so it is the console and Sega’s hardware line that died, not the company.[^2][^25]

place: Video game console · Tokyo and San Francisco
title: Sega Dreamcast (1998–2001): post-mortem · Spectre Brands
description: A record launch, a built-in modem and 510 days from 9/9/99 to the exit: a sourced post-mortem of the Sega Dreamcast, from Sega’s own annual reports, contemporary press and the archived website.

card.blurb: The first console with a modem in the box had the biggest launch day the industry had seen. Sixteen months later Sega stopped making it and never built a console again.

stat.label: from U.S. launch to the exit

hero.dates: Launched in Japan Nov 27, 1998 and in North America Sep 9, 1999. Cancelled Jan 31, 2001.
hero.standfirst: The slogan was “It’s thinking.” By the time the PlayStation 2 arrived, so were its customers.
hero.deck: Sega’s last console came with a modem, a record first day and the best sports games of its generation. It also came from a company that lost money in every year of the console’s life, had lost Electronic Arts, and was selling into the shadow of a rival that was not yet on shelves. This post-mortem is built from Sega’s annual reports, wire and trade coverage from 1999 to 2001, later interviews with the people who ran it, and the archived sega.com.

findings.title: The launch worked. The second Christmas did not.
findings.text: Sega sold 4.65 million consoles in the year to March 2000 and 3.39 million in the next, which its annual report said “fell far short of targets.”[^1][^2]

findings.title: It lost to a console that was barely in stores.
findings.text: The Associated Press reported on the day of the exit that U.S. game fans had given up on the machine in favour of the PlayStation 2, which had then sold about 6.4 million units worldwide.[^4]

findings.title: Sega could not afford a long fight.
findings.text: The company lost money in each of the three fiscal years to March 2000, and another ¥51.7 billion in the year it quit.[^1][^2]

findings.title: The biggest sports publisher stayed away.
findings.text: Electronic Arts never released a Dreamcast game. Sega built the 2K sports line instead and sold it to Take-Two for about $24 million in 2005.[^7][^26]

findings.title: One man’s shares softened the landing.
findings.text: Chairman Isao Okawa gave Sega assets that produced a ¥77.9 billion gain, more than the ¥52.4 billion inventory write-off.[^2]
